This was incredibly thrilling to play. The push for speed challenged your ability to retain information in a short period of time, and it was an incredible experience. It's not real coding, like others have mentioned, so you're not going to learn anything. You essentially learn how to use prebuilt tools in a command prompt and how to communicate with a computer. But it works like a virtual machine with its own language and a fake operating system. (And I think that's really cool). It's also pretty cool that you can see your actual computer's command prompt when you minimize the game, essentially seeing how this virtual machine is talking to your computer.

However, there are gripes.

The ability to lock yourself out of beating the game without knowing it is really easy. You have to be VERY mindful of your actions. Deleting the wrong thing can trap you and force you to start a new game entirely.  

There are also some bugs, mostly involving how the quest system operates. That can also get stuck, especially if you already have a grasp of what you need to do, you can outrun your quest and cause it to lock up. Pace yourself.

Lastly, having content that is procedurally generated is awesome, but I felt like the game struggled between being "open world" and linear. If you want a game where you can investigate to find the story, open world is a wonderful option, but a linear story is great too if you're immersive enough.

Overall, if you want an experience that's an "idea" of hacking, you should definitely try this game.

If the developers make another game like this, I'd be interested in playing that one too. Maybe a sequel? I love the concept, but I'd really hope for a more open world experience.

Hacknet feels like sitting at a computer late at night trying to solve something you are not supposed to see. You spend most of the game in a terminal, typing commands and figuring things out step by step. At first it feels confusing, then it clicks, and that feels good. The story comes through emails and small details, which makes it feel personal instead of forced. There is no rush. You think, try, fail, and learn. The simple visuals keep you focused on the work. If you like puzzles, investigation, and learning systems by doing, Hacknet is easy to get pulled into.

Hacknet
.
Amazing and absolutely unique game!
.
Controls:
Mouse and typing in terminal.
.
Commands:
probe - analyze security
PortHack - hack a computer
Scan - find new computers
cd bin - search for useful executables
ls - view content in current folder
cd .. - go to previous folder
rm [filename] - delete a file
rm * - delete all files
dc - disconnect
help - list all commands
scp [filename] - copies file named [filename] to (/bin default)
ps - lists processes and their PIDs
kill [PID] - kills process number [PID]
mv [FILE] [DESTINATION] - moves or renames a file
connect [ip] - connect to an external computer
cat [filename] - navigate and read file
.
Mechanics and features:
You enter your username, password, and confirm the password.
Scan the network to find new computers.
Hack computers and access files.
You receive mail with missions to accomplish.

Hacknet is an okay game, but it gets repetitive quickly. If you're unable 
to suspend your disbelief, this game might not be for you.

That being said, Hacknet does have some redeeming qualities. The game can 
serve as a tool for learning basic Linux commands, as the game involves 
spamming common terminal commands like, ls, cd, rm and scp.

Additionally, I enjoyed the creative liberties taken in the game's 
"hacking" mechanics. For example, I liked the ability to hack a fake 
cookie clicker and achieve a top score.
The actual hacking tools feel disengaging -- "SSHCrack 22 -> wait 5 seconds for it to finish "cracking" -> Porthack -> wait for it to finish "hacking" -> youre in.

Overall, while Hacknet has some interesting elements, it ultimately feels 
like a shallow experience with limited replay value.
